strengths: Clear and intuitive motivation: The paper addresses a well-known failure mode of standard test-time scaling (majority voting) in mathematical verification. Since mathematical proofs require rigorous correctness across every step, asymmetric 'pessimistic' aggregation (where detecting a single fatal flaw invalidates the proof) is logically sound and well-justified.

Well-designed workflows: The proposed progressive verification framework effectively blends whole-proof evaluation with hierarchical chunk subdivision, enabling efficient early pruning of erroneous proofs and favorable token-efficiency compared to scaling chain-of-thought length.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The authors evaluate multiple contemporary reasoning architectures (GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, DeepSeek-V3.2, Gemini-2.5, Qwen3 variants) across three distinct contest-level benchmarks, showing consistent gains in true negative rate (TNR) and balanced F1.

Valuable qualitative case studies: Section 3.4 and the Appendix provide meticulous manual analyses of false negatives, revealing that many supposed LLM errors in benchmarks like IMO-GradingBench were actually genuine mathematical flaws overlooked by human annotators.
weaknesses: Circular evaluation on QiuZhen-Bench: For QiuZhen-Bench, ground-truth verification labels were generated using GPT-5 with the proposed progressive@3/6 method itself. Evaluating verification techniques against labels produced by the exact method under test introduces severe self-confirmation bias and weakens the benchmark's reliability.

Moderate conceptual novelty: The core idea of pessimistic aggregation for verification has been explored in prior work (e.g., Liu et al., 2025; Pandit et al., 2025). The primary contributions here are prompt-based chunking and hierarchical subdivision heuristics.

Lack of detailed numerical reporting: Most experimental results (e.g., Figures 1, 5, and 6) are presented exclusively as bar charts and line plots without exact numerical tables, error bars, or repeated run variances.

Presentation and polish: The manuscript contains multiple typographical and informal phrasing errors (e.g., 'homemade collection', 'Prarllel review', 'fron QiuZhen college', 'vast experiments') that should be edited for conference presentation standard.

strengths: Identifies a genuine and practical failure mode in LLM proof verification: standard majority voting fails on verification because error identification is a sparse, needle-in-a-haystack problem where consensus often favors sycophantic false acceptance.

Proposes clear, structured workflow variants—specifically the hierarchical progressive pessimistic verification with early exit/pruning, which optimizes token cost and runtime latency compared to unpruned parallel sweeps.
Conducts experiments across an impressive and diverse collection of frontier and open-weight models (GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash, Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeek-v3.2, Qwen3 variants).

Provides valuable qualitative case studies on benchmark data quality, demonstrating with concrete mathematical examples that frontier verifiers frequently flag genuine mathematical gaps or incorrect steps that were overlooked in human-annotated datasets like IMO-GradingBench.
weaknesses: Severe circularity in benchmark construction for QiuZhen-Bench: As described in Section 3.1, ground-truth labels for QiuZhen-Bench were generated using GPT-5 with progressive@3/6—the very method under study. Evaluating verification methods against silver labels generated by a pessimistic verifier introduces confirmation bias and invalidates claims of benchmark rigor.

Metric inflation and lack of threshold calibration: The paper primarily reports Balanced F1 (harmonic mean of TPR and TNR). In regimes where baseline TNR is extremely low and TPR is high, any aggressively strict/pessimistic rule mechanically shifts the operating point to boost TNR, artificially inflating the harmonic mean. A complete ROC or Precision-Recall analysis across varying voting thresholds is missing.

High vulnerability to hallucinated criticisms in smaller/open models: The 'reject if any check fails' rule compounds model hallucinations. As Table 1 shows, 13 out of 15 false negatives produced by Qwen3-30B-A3B were classified as 'nonsense'. While frontier models may have low error hallucination rates, the method drastically degrades TPR and precision on non-frontier models without a mechanism to filter spurious critiques.

Limited conceptual novelty: The core idea of pessimistic verification (unanimous agreement required for correctness) is already known (e.g., Liu et al., 2025). The vertical and progressive variations largely represent standard chunking and hierarchical divide-and-conquer strategies applied to proof text.

Presentation flaws and compilation artifacts: The manuscript contains multiple typographical and formatting errors, including mathematical rendering bugs (e.g., '$c\ e1$' instead of '$c \neq 1$', '$A\ eq0$', '$Ai\ ot \subseteq Cf$'), spelling mistakes ('Prarllel' in Figure 2, 'drasticly' on p. 4, 'fron' on p. 2/13, 'conpetitions' on p. 5), and under-specified subsampling protocols for IMO-GradingBench.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely challenge: detecting subtle errors in natural language proofs where standard test-time scaling strategies like majority voting fail.
Proposes intuitive, modular workflows—vertical chunking and progressive multi-scale verification—that decompose long, complex mathematical proofs into manageable verification tasks.

Includes a detailed qualitative case study on false negatives (Section 3.4 and Appendix A.3), demonstrating that frontier models under pessimistic checking frequently surface valid mathematical flaws overlooked in benchmark annotations.
Evaluates a wide spectrum of contemporary open and proprietary models ranging from small scale (Qwen 1.7B/4B) to frontier reasoning models (GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro).
weaknesses: Severe circularity in QiuZhen-Bench evaluation: In Section 3.1, the authors state that QiuZhen-Bench labels were produced using GPT-5 with the proposed 'progressive@3/6' workflow. Evaluating progressive verification against ground-truth labels defined by the exact same progressive verification setup creates significant evaluation bias.

Lack of thresholding and calibration baselines: Pessimistic verification fundamentally operates as an extreme classification threshold (predicting 'correct' if and only if all samples pass). The manuscript does not compare this against standard single-pass probability/logit thresholding or prompts calibrated to varying degrees of strictness, leaving it unclear whether performance gains reflect true reasoning capability or simple threshold tuning.

Severe false-alarm amplification for non-frontier models: While frontier models occasionally catch subtle bugs, Table 1 reveals that 13 out of 15 false negative judgments by Qwen3-30B were classified as 'Nonsense'. Applying an unweighted logical-AND over noisy runs drastically inflates hallucinated errors for open-weight/smaller models.

Flawed efficiency metrics: The compute efficiency analysis in Figure 1 uses commercial API token prices ('input_tokens / 8 + output_tokens') rather than hardware-grounded computational measures (such as FLOPs, total generated tokens, or latency), making claims about outperforming long-CoT test-time scaling misleading.

Presentation flaws and transcription issues: The manuscript contains notable typographical and formatting defects, including repeated misspellings ('conpetitions', 'drasticly', 'fron QiuZhen college') and corrupted mathematical notations in the appendix (e.g., 'A eq0', 'c e1', 'c e0' instead of proper inequality symbols on pages 27–29).

strengths: Addresses an important and timely challenge in LLM reasoning: the high cost and unreliability of automated verification for open-ended, natural language mathematical proofs.

The progressive decomposition strategy (hierarchical bisection combined with early-exit pruning) is intuitive, effective, and provides significant token efficiency gains over naive repeated verification and standard long CoT scaling.

The qualitative error analysis and case studies on IMO-GradingBench are insightful, convincingly demonstrating that many benchmark 'false negatives' are actually genuine mathematical errors overlooked by human annotators.
Experiments span a broad suite of models (GPT, Gemini, Claude, and Qwen families) across multiple verification datasets and downstream agentic solving workflows.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is relatively incremental: the pessimistic rule (marking a solution invalid if any verifier finds a flaw) combined with chunking/bisection is conceptually straightforward.

The downstream agentic problem-solving evaluation relies on very small sample sizes (6 problems from IMO 2025 and 12 problems from MathArena Apex 2025), which limits the statistical significance of the solving claims despite repeating runs.
The QiuZhen-Bench relies on LLM (GPT-5) generation and annotation without systematic expert validation, which introduces potential model biases and circularity in evaluation.

The paper notes instances where correct solutions were erroneously modified during the iterative repair loop due to false alarms; the trade-offs between hyper-pessimism and search derailment in agentic workflows deserve deeper quantitative analysis.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental bottleneck in test-time scaling and agentic workflows for mathematical reasoning: informal proof verification and the asymmetry of error detection.

The proposed progressive pessimistic verification combines hierarchical proof decomposition with early exit/pruning, offering a principled and significantly more token-efficient alternative to naive parallel verification or extended long CoT.

Provides a insightful qualitative and quantitative case study revealing substantial label noise in standard benchmarks (e.g., IMO-GradingBench), demonstrating that many alleged 'false negatives' from frontier models actually identify genuine mathematical flaws overlooked by human annotators.
Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple frontier model families (GPT-5, Gemini 3, Qwen 3) on both verification benchmarks and full problem-solving pipelines (IMO 2025, MathArena Apex 2025).
weaknesses: From an algorithmic perspective, the concepts of pessimistic verification (unanimous agreement required for acceptance) and hierarchical chunk decomposition are relatively standard pruning and divide-and-conquer paradigms.

QiuZhen-Bench annotations rely heavily on LLM (GPT-5) self-labeling, which risks circularity and model bias, particularly given the paper's thesis regarding LLM verification unreliability and benchmark annotation fragility.

The downstream agentic problem-solving experiments are evaluated on relatively small test sets (6 problems for IMO 2025, 12 problems for Apex 2025), which leaves room for variance despite repeated trials.

strengths: Addresses an important and pressing bottleneck: automated verification of informal, open-ended mathematical proofs, which is crucial for test-time scaling and self-correcting agentic workflows.

The proposed progressive pessimistic verification combines multi-scale proof chunking with early rejection/pruning, achieving a superior balance between True Negative Rate (error detection) and computational token efficiency compared to standard long CoT and naive repeated verification.

Includes a valuable and insightful critical analysis of existing benchmarks (IMO-GradingBench, Hard2Verify), demonstrating through detailed manual case studies (Appendix A.4) that many apparent 'false negatives' by strong LLMs are actually legitimate catches of subtle mathematical errors overlooked by human annotators.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning a wide range of model scales and families, demonstrating consistent improvements in Balanced F1 across benchmarks and showing practical gains on downstream problem-solving tasks (IMO 2025 and MathArena Apex 2025).
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is relatively modest: pessimistic ensembling (a logical OR over error flags) and chunk-based inspection are natural heuristics in verification and software testing, representing an engineering refinement rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic paradigm.

High susceptibility to false alarms on weaker verifiers: because any flagged error causes rejection, verifiers prone to hallucinating errors (as seen in Table 2 where Qwen3-30B produced 18/20 'nonsense' false negatives) suffer severe TPR degradation, and the paper lacks a principled mechanism or confidence calibration to mitigate this failure mode.

The chunking mechanism splits proofs arbitrarily by line count (k lines) rather than logical mathematical steps or semantic blocks, which risks cutting mathematical statements or derivations mid-stride and inducing spurious verification failures.

Limited sample size in the agentic problem-solving experiments (IMO 2025 has only 6 problems; Apex 2025 has 12), which limits the statistical significance of the downstream iterative solving findings despite repeated trials.
Reproducibility concerns arising from heavy reliance on proprietary or preview model checkpoints (such as GPT-5, Gemini 3 Pro Preview) and synthetic LLM-labeled testbeds (QiuZhen-Bench).
